summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style overview of Detroit, Michigan, covering its mayors and politics, geography and metro area, demographics and segregation trends, music history, major medical institutions, neighborhoods and redevelopment, and its founding by French settlers and the 1943 race riot. It moves from civic governance and modern redevelopment to historical settlement and migration, with the 1943 riot as a key event.
one_line: Overview of Detroit, Michigan, covering its government, metro area, demographics, music heritage, medical institutions, redevelopment, and history.
key_facts: Detroit has had a total of 74 mayors since its incorporation in 1802.
Louis Miriani, served from 1957 to 1962, was Detroit's last mayor from the Republican Party.
In 1973, Detroit elected its first black mayor, Coleman Young, who served five terms.
Detroit is the most populous city in Michigan and the largest city on the United States–Canada border.
Metro Detroit is home to 5.3 million people, the second-largest metropolitan area in the Midwestern United States behind Chicago.
In 2010, Blacks/African-Americans made up nearly 82 percent of Detroit's population, compared with 13 percent of Michigan's population.
The number of integrated neighborhoods in Detroit increased from 100 in 2000 to 204 in 2010.
The Detroit Medical Center has more than 2,000 licensed beds and 3,000 affiliated physicians and is the largest private employer in the City of Detroit.
Campus Martius, a reconfigured downtown park, opened in 2004 and has been cited as one of the best public spaces in the United States.
Detroit's city government has a nine-member city council and has operated as a 'strong mayoral' system since voters approved the charter in 1974.
In 1701, Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac and about fifty-one French settlers founded Fort Pontchartrain du Détroit.
By 1778, Detroit's population reached 2,144 and it was the third-largest city in the Province of Quebec.
The Detroit race riot of 1943 occurred three weeks after the Packard plant protest and killed 34 people, 25 of them African American.
Around 25,000 white workers walked off the job at Packard in June 1943 after three Black workers were promoted to assembly lines alongside whites.
John Lee Hooker became a long-term resident of Detroit's southwest Delray neighborhood in the 1940s and recorded for Fortune Records.
